_comment: The Python canon: the pragmatism of the .NET platform canon (dotnet-canon, dotnet-decisions), translated to Python from sources that agree - PEPs 8/20/257/544/585/604/695/735/749, the Python docs and devguide, Google's Python style guide, the mypy, pytest, import-linter, ruff and Pydantic docs, the Scientific Python development guide, Architecture Patterns with Python, Hynek Schlawack, Mark Seemann, Martin Fowler, J.B. Rainsberger and Microsoft's architecture guide - researched 2026-10-04. Most were adopted in okl #116, #118 and #120; the five added in #132 (runtime Protocol checks, the composition root, value objects at seams, contract tests, typing syntax by floor) are researched, not adopted: okl's own CI does not run its Postgres contract. Rules that only make sense in Python set applies_to 'python'; the language-neutral ones leave it unset. Nothing here claims verification: a citation is not a check. Verify each against your own repo with `okl verify`. `okl init` imports it when it creates a new, empty store in a repo whose stack it detects as python; a repo whose store already holds lessons runs `okl seed python-canon`.

nodes.title: Enforce the dependency rule with an import-linter layers contract: Python's architecture test
nodes.body: The middle step of convention -> architecture test -> package split, in Python. A `layers` contract in pyproject.toml lists the layers top to bottom: a higher layer may import a lower one, never the reverse, and `|` marks siblings that must not import each other either. `lint-imports` in CI fails on the first import that points up and names its line. It needs no package split and no new structure. okl's contract held on its first run; an upward import planted on purpose (store -> client) reported BROKEN with its line number, which is how to prove yours before trusting it. Set `exhaustive = true` (with `containers`) so a module left out of the list is an error, not one the contract silently ignores.
nodes.symptom: a lower module imports a higher one (the store imports the client) and nothing fails
nodes.fix: add a [tool.importlinter] layers contract, run lint-imports in CI, and plant one upward import to watch it go red

nodes.title: Every module, public class and public function has a docstring that lets a reader call it without reading its body
nodes.body: PEP 257: all modules, and every function and class a module exports, have docstrings. Google's Python guide sets the bar: 'A docstring should give enough information to write a call to the function without reading the function's code.' One to three lines is usual: what it is for, and what a caller must know - what it returns, what None or an empty filter means, what it raises, a command's exit codes. Writing Args and Returns only where a name and a type do not explain a parameter is a deliberate departure from Google's guide, which lists every parameter. Enforce presence, not format: ruff D100-D104 with pydocstyle convention = "google". Tests can be exempt: a test reads as its name and its comments.
nodes.symptom: a public function whose purpose and contract can only be learned by reading its body
nodes.fix: select ruff D100-D104 (convention google); write what it is for and what a caller must know

nodes.title: Comment the tricky parts and the reasons; never describe the code
nodes.body: Google's Python guide: 'Never describe the code. Assume the person reading the code knows Python (though not what you're trying to do) better than you do', and 'If you're going to have to explain it at the next code review, you should comment it now.' A comment carries why: the constraint, the incident, the failure a line prevents, a decision and what would change it. A comment that restates the line below it is noise that goes stale. Two tiers work well: teaching-grade comments where a newcomer learns the architecture, and none on plumbing whose names already say what it is.
nodes.symptom: a comment paraphrasing the line below it, or a non-obvious line with no comment at all
nodes.fix: delete what-comments; add a why-comment wherever you would otherwise explain the line in review

nodes.title: Type every signature, and tighten mypy one step at a time, in the order its docs give
nodes.body: Types are documentation a tool checks. Google: at least annotate your public APIs; ruff ANN flags any signature without hints, tests exempt. mypy's guide for an existing codebase gives the order: warn_unused_configs, warn_unused_ignores and warn_redundant_casts; then strict_equality; then check_untyped_defs, which it recommends 'as soon as you can' because without it mypy does not check the bodies of unannotated functions at all; then the disallow_* flags, which together amount to --strict. Each step must be a gate that passes, never a blanket ignore, and enable_error_code = ['ignore-without-code'] makes every type: ignore name the error it silences. In okl, typing the store let mypy check a CLI line it had never checked, and it found a real mismatch there.
nodes.symptom: mypy passes code it never checked, because the functions have no annotations
nodes.fix: ruff ANN on every signature; mypy flags in the documented order; --strict once the public signatures are typed

nodes.found_by: PEPs 585, 604, 695 and 749; the Python typing docs (AnyStr deprecated in 3.13); ruff's pyupgrade rules UP006, UP007, UP035, UP040, UP045, UP046 and UP047, checked on ruff 0.16.8 on 2026-10-04
nodes.title: Write type hints in the newest syntax your Python floor allows, and let ruff's UP rules hold the line
nodes.body: Each syntax has a minimum version: builtin generics such as list[str] (PEP 585) from 3.9; X | None (PEP 604) from 3.10; and the type statement with def f[T]() and class C[T] type parameters (PEP 695) from 3.12, which retire the TypeVar, Generic and TypeAlias boilerplate. Your requires-python decides which apply, not the newest release: a 3.10 floor cannot use PEP 695. ruff's UP rules flag the older forms against its target version: UP006 and UP035 for typing.List-style generics and their imports, UP007 and UP045 for Union and Optional, UP040 for TypeAlias, UP046 and UP047 for generic classes and functions. ruff takes the target from requires-python (a TypeVar function is flagged under >=3.12 and passes under >=3.10), but a [tool.ruff] target-version wins when set, and a stale one silently switches the newer rules off. ruff marks the PEP 695 fixes unsafe: the new syntax infers variance, a type alias cannot be used in isinstance(), and its docs note that not every type checker fully supports PEP 695 yet. Rewrite those by hand and run the one checker that gates CI (py_one_type_checker). typing.AnyStr is deprecated since 3.13 and leaves typing in 3.18: on a 3.12 floor UP047 flags it, and the replacement is a constrained type parameter, def f[T: (str, bytes)](); below 3.12, define TypeVar('AnyStr', str, bytes) yourself. from __future__ import annotations still helps below 3.14, but PEP 749 (Final) plans to deprecate it no sooner than the first release after 3.13's end of life (October 2029), and to remove it at least two releases later. No ruff rule flags it, so remove it yourself in the change that raises requires-python to 3.14.
nodes.symptom: new code written with TypeVar, Optional[...] or List[...] in a repo whose Python floor has the newer syntax
nodes.fix: select ruff's UP rules; delete [tool.ruff] target-version or keep it equal to the requires-python floor; rewrite the PEP 695 forms by hand and re-run your type checker; remove from __future__ import annotations when the floor reaches 3.14

nodes.title: pytest runs strict, and any warning fails the test that raised it
nodes.body: The Scientific Python development guide's configuration: strict markers and strict config (in pytest 9, `strict = true`, which also fails an xfail that starts passing) and filterwarnings = ["error"], because 'Python hides important warnings by default... If you are a developer, you don't want it to be nice.' Deprecation warnings are how a new Python or library version says what it will break. Strict pytest makes them failures on the day they appear, rather than a broken upgrade months later. okl's first strict run found two real problems: Starlette's TestClient deprecating httpx (since 1.2.0), and SQLite connections that were never closed. When a third-party warning has to be tolerated, ignore that one warning by message and category, with a comment, never a whole class of warnings.
nodes.symptom: a deprecation warning scrolls past in CI output for months, then an upgrade breaks
nodes.fix: [tool.pytest.ini_options] strict = true and filterwarnings = ["error"]; narrow, commented ignores only

nodes.title: CI tests every Python version requires-python claims, and dropping one is a dated decision
nodes.body: A version range in pyproject.toml is a promise, and testing one version leaves the rest assumed. okl claimed >=3.10 and tested 3.12 alone. Its first matrix run (3.10 to 3.14) passed only after fixing a failure that appeared on 3.13 and later and nowhere else: SQLite connections that were never closed. Run the suite once per version with fail-fast off, and keep lint, types and coverage on a single version. The devguide gives each version's end-of-life date (3.10's was 2026-10-01); when to drop one is a choice. Some projects drop at end of life, Scientific Python's SPEC 0 drops earlier, and okl still supports 3.10 after its end of life. Whichever you choose, announce it, because it leaves users of that version on older releases.

nodes.fix: a CI matrix over every claimed version with fail-fast: false; decide, and announce, when to drop one

nodes.title: Functions stay inside pylint's limits, and a module nobody can read end to end is split by responsibility
nodes.body: Google: 'If a function exceeds about 40 lines, think about whether it can be broken up without harming the structure of the program.' The usual gate is pylint's thresholds, through ruff: PLR0911 (6 returns), PLR0912 (12 branches), PLR0915 (50 statements) and PLR0917 (5 positional arguments). Use PLR0917 rather than PLR0913, which counts every argument: keyword-only parameters read fine at the call site, and six positional values do not. No source agrees on a number for a whole file. Split a module that holds several responsibilities into a package with one module per responsibility, not into technical layers: okl's 1,648-line cli.py became cli/, with one module per command group. A declarative table such as an argparse tree may stay long, as long as its exemption states the reason on the same line.
nodes.symptom: a function you have to scroll to follow, or a module nobody reads end to end
nodes.fix: ruff PLR0911/0912/0915/0917; split by responsibility; any justified exemption states its reason inline

nodes.title: Avoid metaclasses, reflection and __del__: longer, straightforward code reads better
nodes.body: Google's section on power features says to avoid custom metaclasses, bytecode access, dynamic inheritance, reflection such as dispatching on getattr, and __del__. Its reason: 'It's harder to read, understand, and debug code that's using unusual features underneath', so code 'that is longer but is straightforward' wins. PEP 20 agrees: explicit is better than implicit, and if the implementation is hard to explain, it's a bad idea. Use an explicit dispatch table instead of getattr on a name, weakref.finalize instead of __del__, and a dataclass instead of a metaclass.

nodes.fix: replace it with the explicit form; where one is genuinely needed, comment why at its definition

nodes.title: Errors flow as specific exceptions, turned into exit codes or responses at the edge; no catch-all without a stated reason
nodes.body: Python's error idiom is exceptions (the glossary's EAFP), so this is Python's form of picking one way for errors to flow. Raise a specific exception, with a message that says what to do, where the problem is found. Catch it once, at the edge: a CLI turns it into an exit code (okl: 0 clean, 1 findings, 2 could not run), and a service turns it into a 4xx. PEP 20: 'Errors should never pass silently. Unless explicitly silenced.' ruff BLE001 flags a catch-all `except Exception` that neither re-raises nor logs the exception; giving the reason beside its noqa is a convention ruff does not check (a bare `except:` is E722). Result-style return values are not idiomatic Python, so do not mix them in.
nodes.symptom: an except Exception that swallows an error, or a caller's mistake reported as an outage
nodes.fix: specific exceptions, one place at the edge that translates them, and ruff BLE001 with a stated reason for every catch-all

nodes.found_by: Hynek Schlawack, 'Don't Mock What You Don't Own in 5 Minutes' (hynek.me/articles/what-to-mock-in-5-mins/, 2022); Freeman and Pryce, Growing Object-Oriented Software
nodes.title: Mock only your own objects: wrap a third-party API in a thin adapter you own, and fake that
nodes.body: Hynek Schlawack: whenever you use mock objects, 'use them to substitute your own objects and not third-party ones.' A mock of a library you do not own encodes your guess about how it behaves, and it keeps passing after the library changes. Put the third-party call behind a small adapter that has the interface your code wants. Test the adapter against the real thing (an in-process server or a container), and use a fake of the adapter everywhere else. In Python the adapter's interface can be a typing.Protocol, which needs no inheritance.
nodes.symptom: a test patches a library's internals and keeps passing while the real call is broken
nodes.fix: own an adapter, test it against the real dependency, and fake the adapter in unit tests

nodes.title: Start with a function; use a class when state and behaviour travel together, and a Protocol only when something substitutes it
nodes.body: The Python form of 'interfaces earn their keep through consumer substitution'. Architecture Patterns with Python, the book that teaches these patterns, lists their cost: 'Any extra layer of indirection always increases maintenance costs and adds a "WTF factor" for Python programmers who've never seen the Repository pattern before', and 'If your app is just a simple CRUD (create-read-update-delete) wrapper around a database, then you don't need a domain model or a repository.' Prefer composition to inheritance (Hynek, 'Subclassing in Python Redux'). Use a dataclass for a record, and a typing.Protocol (PEP 544) for a port, because structural typing lets a test fake satisfy it without inheriting anything. A class with only __init__ and one method is a function.

nodes.fix: inline it as a function or a dataclass; introduce a Protocol when a second implementation or a test fake needs one

nodes.title: isinstance() against a Protocol checks names, not signatures: conformance comes from the type checker and a shared test
nodes.body: The Python docs: @runtime_checkable 'will check only the presence of the required methods or attributes, not their type signatures or types.' mypy's docs say the same ('signatures of methods are not checked'), and PEP 544 likens the check to a hasattr() per member. Pydantic inherits the gap: with arbitrary_types_allowed, a field typed with a Protocol is validated by 'a simple check of instance type', and 'nothing in the instance of the arbitrary type is checked'. Reproduced on a published example that offered @runtime_checkable plus a Pydantic model as an extra safety layer: an invoke(a, b, c, d) that returns 42 passed both, and a LangChain chat model passed both, then answered with an AIMessage where the Protocol promised str. The type checker rejected both, and also caught the example's own pipeline passing a PromptValue where its Protocol took str. So a runtime check says an object has the right names, never that it fits. What makes an implementation fit is the type checker over the code that wires it in, plus one behaviour test that every implementation, real or fake, runs.
nodes.symptom: an isinstance() check against a Protocol, or a Pydantic field typed with one, treated as proof that an implementation fits
nodes.fix: type-check the code that wires implementations in; run one shared behaviour test over every implementation; trust isinstance on a Protocol for what it checks, that the members exist, and never as proof of signatures, types or behaviour

nodes.found_by: Mark Seemann, 'Composition Root' (blog.ploeh.dk, 2011); Architecture Patterns with Python, ch. 13 'Dependency Injection (and Bootstrapping)' (Percival and Gregory, cosmicpython.com); the import-linter docs (protected contracts, added in 2.5), checked with import-linter 2.15 on 2026-10-04
nodes.title: Build the adapters (clients, connections, repositories) in one place near the entry point and pass them in; business code never constructs its own
nodes.body: Seemann: 'A Composition Root is a (preferably) unique location in an application where modules are composed together', placed 'as close as possible to the application's entry point', and 'Only applications should have Composition Roots. Libraries and frameworks shouldn't.' Architecture Patterns with Python calls it 'a bootstrap script to you and me' and does 'manual DI' (dependency injection without a framework): its bootstrap function builds the real adapters and hands them to the handlers that use them, so a test can hand in a fake instead. Pass each adapter in as a parameter, of a function or a constructor. Type it with a Protocol where a fake or a second implementation substitutes it (py_classes_earn_place), and with the concrete class otherwise. The book suggests a DI framework only 'if you find yourself wanting to do DI in more things and at different times, or if you ever get into dependency chains'; until then the root is a plain function that calls constructors. A root that is only named in a document drifts. An import-linter protected contract (import-linter 2.5 and later), with the adapter package in protected_modules and the root as the only allowed_importers, fails CI on the first stray import. A forbidden contract cannot say this: it also follows indirect imports, so the entry point that imports the root breaks it even when the wiring is right.
nodes.symptom: a business-logic class that builds its own client or connection from environment variables, or adapter imports scattered through the code
nodes.fix: write one bootstrap() function, called from the entry point, that builds every client and connection and passes them in as arguments; consider a DI framework once you inject in many places or dependencies have dependencies of their own; an import-linter protected contract with the root as the only allowed importer keeps the adapters out of everything else, so plant one stray import and watch it go red

nodes.found_by: Architecture Patterns with Python, ch. 1 (value objects as frozen dataclasses); the Python dataclasses docs, 'Frozen instances'; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, 'Anti-Corruption Layer pattern', after Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design
nodes.title: Values a provider hands you become frozen dataclasses you own; the provider's format is translated inside its adapter and goes no further
nodes.body: A seam here is the boundary between your code and a provider's client: an LLM SDK, a vector store, an HTTP API. Architecture Patterns with Python: 'A value object is any domain object that is uniquely identified by the data it holds; we usually make them immutable', written as @dataclass(frozen=True). Any dataclass compares by value; frozen=True also refuses assignment to fields and makes instances hashable. The Python docs state the limit: 'It is not possible to create truly immutable Python objects'. A list inside a frozen dataclass can still be changed in place, and hashing the instance raises TypeError: unhashable type: 'list', so use tuples and frozensets for its collections. This is for values, data without identity. An entity your own code changes over time stays an ordinary class: the book's repository hands back a mutable Batch. The anti-corruption layer (Evans, in Microsoft's architecture guide) is where translation lives: it 'contains all the logic necessary to translate between the two systems', so the provider's model never leaks past its adapter, and changing provider rewrites one translation rather than every caller.
nodes.symptom: callers read a provider's raw response fields, or a 'frozen' value is changed through a list it holds
nodes.fix: inside each adapter, translate the provider's payload into frozen dataclasses you own, with tuples for their collections; entities your own code changes stay ordinary classes

nodes.found_by: Martin Fowler, 'ContractTest' (martinfowler.com/bliki, 2011); J.B. Rainsberger, 'Getting Started with Contract Tests' (blog.thecodewhisperer.com, 2017); okl's _backend_conformance (tests/test_okl.py), one helper body called once per backend, whose Postgres call runs only when OKL_TEST_POSTGRES_URL is set
nodes.title: Every implementation of an interface (a Protocol in Python), fakes included, runs one shared contract test
nodes.body: A type checker run over the code that wires implementations in, and over the tests that pass fakes, proves the signatures fit. It cannot prove a fake behaves like the real thing, and logic tests that only ever run against fakes keep passing while the real adapter is broken. Fowler's contract tests 'check that all the calls against your test doubles return the same results as a call to the external service would'. Rainsberger writes them once against the interface and runs them against every implementation: a contract test 'describes behavior that clients rely on without referring to a specific implementation of the collaborator'. In pytest that is one test module with a fixture parametrized over the implementations (@pytest.fixture(params=[...])): the fake on every run, the real adapter against a real local instance (a container for a database), and the live service on a schedule. Recorded responses check your parsing, not the provider, so they cannot tell you the provider changed. The .NET canon's Testcontainers decision is the same lesson for databases: the contract runs against a real container, never an in-memory provider or a SQLite stand-in. okl shares one body (_backend_conformance) between its SQLite and Postgres backends, after the Postgres one matched every signature and returned unranked results. Its Postgres run is opt-in (OKL_TEST_POSTGRES_URL) and CI starts no Postgres server, so that half proves nothing until something runs it, which is the gap this lesson is about.
nodes.symptom: unit tests pass against a fake while the real adapter is broken, or two implementations with the same signatures return different results
nodes.fix: one contract test module per interface, parametrized over every implementation including the fake; run the real adapter against a real local instance (a container for a database) and the live service on a schedule; recorded responses check your parsing, not the provider

nodes.found_by: Python Logging HOWTO, 'Configuring Logging for a Library'; adopted in okl #118 (ruff T20)
nodes.title: Library code never prints; output belongs to the command-line layer
nodes.body: Python's logging HOWTO: a library leaves logging configuration to the application (it configures nothing; at most it adds a NullHandler). The same goes for print: a module that prints cannot be used by a service, an MCP server or a test without its output leaking into theirs. Enforce it with ruff T20, with per-file-ignores naming the command-line layers. When logging, pass values as arguments rather than f-strings (ruff G004), so the message is only formatted when a record is actually emitted.
nodes.symptom: a print() in a module that services or tests import
nodes.fix: return the text or raise; print only in the CLI layer; ruff T20 with per-file-ignores for that layer

nodes.found_by: PEP 735 (dependency groups); the Python Packaging User Guide; okl's rule on pinning CI gate tools; adopted in okl for its own dev tools (#121)
nodes.title: pyproject.toml is the one home for versions: ranges for what users install, exact pins for the tools that gate CI
nodes.body: The Python form of 'all package versions live in one central file'. Runtime dependencies take ranges, because a published package has to coexist with its users' other dependencies. The lint, type and test tools that gate CI are pinned exactly, after checking that the version exists on PyPI, so a new release cannot fail a branch that changed nothing. Dev tools belong in a dependency group (PEP 735), not in a published extra users can install. An application also commits a lock file, so its installs are reproducible.
nodes.symptom: a tool version pinned in a workflow file, or dev tools shipped as an installable extra
nodes.fix: versions only in pyproject.toml; exact pins for gate tools; dev tools in [dependency-groups]

nodes.title: Gate CI on one type checker, and write down what would make you switch
nodes.body: Credible sources disagree on which type checker is best, and the field moves fast. mypy is the reference implementation; pyright, pyrefly (stable since its 1.0 in May 2026) and Astral's ty (in beta since December 2025) are faster, and the typing project's conformance suite tracks how fully each one implements the typing spec. Which you pick matters less than gating CI on exactly one, so its findings mean something, and writing down the trigger that would make you switch (a check you need, a speed you need, a checker reaching stable), so the choice is revisited on evidence rather than fashion.
nodes.symptom: two type checkers disagreeing in CI, or a proposal to switch checkers with no stated reason
nodes.fix: one checker gates CI; record the trigger that would make you switch, and revisit when it fires

nodes.title: Pick one docstring format, and enforce that docstrings exist before enforcing their sections
nodes.body: Google, NumPy and Sphinx (reST) styles all have large followings, and PEP 257 prescribes none of them. Pick one and tell the linter (ruff's pydocstyle `convention`). Enforce presence first (ruff D100-D104): that is what makes a codebase followable. The section rules (D405-D417) mostly produce churn over formatting rather than understanding, so add them when generated API docs become a deliverable.

nodes.fix: one format, set as ruff's pydocstyle convention; enforce D100-D104; add the section rules only for generated API docs
